meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They're Cheering Us Both, You Because Nobody Understands You, and Me Because Everybody Understands Me'?
meta.ogDescription: Einstein was the target of the joke, not its author. Chaplin gets the credit — but the wording is second-hand from a 1947 memoir.

answer.label: Not Einstein — Chaplin said it, and even that is second-hand
answer.authorDates: 1889–1977 · English comic actor, filmmaker and composer
answer.sourceLine: Einstein is the subject of this joke, not its author — he is the one nobody understands. The words are given to Chaplin, and the wording everyone quotes comes from János: The Story of a Doctor (1947), the memoir of Einstein’s physician and friend János Plesch, who was not present when it was said. Chaplin’s own account of the evening, published in 1933, tells it differently and credits the observation about their two kinds of fame to Einstein’s son. Quote Investigator ↗ treats Chaplin’s first-hand version as the stronger evidence and calls the Plesch anecdote “probably inaccurate”.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the popular credit is to the wrong man, and the famous wording rests on a second-hand memoir.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Charles Chaplin, “A Comedian Sees the World – Part II”, October 1933, p. 17 — in which the remark is credited to Einstein’s son
János: The Story of a Doctor
Usually attached to the gala premiere of City Lights, Los Angeles Theatre, 30 January 1931, where Einstein and his wife were guests of honour

source.excerpt: As the people on the sidewalks recognized two of their greatest, if very different, contemporaries, they gave them a tremendous reception which greatly astonished Einstein. “They’re cheering us both,” said Chaplin: “you because nobody understands you, and me because everybody understands me.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ establishes that the earliest evidence is Chaplin’s own article in Woman’s Home Companion for October 1933, and that in it “Chaplin credited the crucially insightful statement about fame to Einstein’s son”. QI had the magazine page checked at the Spokane Public Library.

The wording people actually quote enters the record in 1947, in János: The Story of a Doctor by János Plesch ↗, translated by Edward Fitzgerald (Victor Gollancz, London), p. 211. QI verified that page from scans ↗ and notes that Plesch “was not present when the words were spoken, so his account was second-hand”.

From there it spreads through the Einstein literature rather than out of it. Carl Seelig’s Albert Einstein: A Documentary Biography (1956) reproduces it and cites Plesch by name; Denis Brian’s Einstein: A Life (1996) carries it with reference notes pointing back to Seelig; Walter Isaacson’s Einstein: His Life and Universe (2007) footnotes Seelig and Brian. Every later telling traces to the same second-hand source.

Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein ↗ files the line under “Others on Einstein” rather than among his own words — the correct shelf, since the joke is about him. The premiere it is usually attached to is real: City Lights opened in Los Angeles on 30 January 1931 ↗ with Einstein and his wife as guests of honour.
source.cutTag: János Plesch, 1947 — the wording everyone quotes
source.excerptNote: Plesch was Einstein’s doctor and friend, but he was not in the car. Chaplin was, and fourteen years earlier he had published his own version of the evening — in which the observation is not his at all: “You are popular,” he said, “because you are understood by the masses. On the other hand, the professor’s popularity with the masses is because he is not understood.” The speaker there is one of Einstein’s two sons. Chaplin does not say which, and neither does anyone since.

source.rightsNote: The sentence in its familiar wording was first published in 1947, in Edward Fitzgerald’s English translation of János Plesch’s memoir. That is well after the 1931 cut-off for the United States public domain, so we treat both the book and its translation as in copyright. Chaplin’s differently-worded 1933 magazine account is a separate publication with its own rights.

author.name: Charlie Chaplin
author.heading: About Charlie Chaplin
author.metaLine: 1889–1977 · English comic actor, filmmaker and composer
author.bio: Chaplin was, by 1931, the most recognisable human being on earth — a silent comedian whose Tramp needed no translation, which is precisely the asymmetry this joke turns on. He was also a working writer, and the 1933 travel series he published in Woman’s Home Companion is why we can check this story at all: it is the only account of the evening by someone who was actually in the room, and in it he hands the good line to somebody else.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one is passed around as an Einstein quotation, which gets the joke exactly backwards, and the chain of custody is longer than it looks.

items.why: Einstein does not speak in any version of this story. He is the man being told that the crowd cheers him because nobody understands him. Attributing it to him inverts the joke and removes the only person it is about.

Chaplin is the speaker in Plesch’s 1947 memoir and in every biography that follows it. But Plesch was not there, and Chaplin’s own first-hand account from 1933 does not claim the line — QI concludes the Plesch anecdote “was probably inaccurate” ↗.

In Woman’s Home Companion, October 1933, Chaplin writes that during dinner at the Einsteins’ flat “his son remarked on the psychology of the popularity of Einstein and myself”, and quotes him. Einstein had two sons, Hans Albert and Eduard; QI notes it does not know which one Chaplin meant ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The safest true statement is the narrow one: the observation was made in Einstein’s company, about Einstein, by someone who was not Einstein — and the earliest witness to it, Chaplin, did not claim it for himself.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By 1931 Einstein was famous in a way no scientist had been before: not admired for a result anyone could follow, but recognised on sight, mobbed on sidewalks, invited to film premieres as a draw. The joke is funny because it names the strange thing about that fame without being unkind about it — two men getting the same ovation for opposite reasons.

It is also a small case study in how a good line drifts. Chaplin printed his account first and gave the credit away. A second-hand retelling fourteen years later gave it to Chaplin, in tighter and more quotable words, and that version is the one the biographies picked up and the internet eventually reassigned to Einstein — the one man in the story who certainly did not say it.
detailsBody: Chaplin’s 1933 telling is domestic rather than glamorous. He describes returning Einstein’s earlier visit by calling at the family’s “modest flat”, meeting Einstein’s wife, his daughter and his son, and eating home-baked tarts made by Mrs Einstein. A group of Japanese children danced; one of them asked both men for autographs, and Chaplin drew his oversized shoes while Einstein wrote out an equation. It is in that setting, over dinner, that the remark about their two kinds of popularity is made — by Einstein’s son.

Plesch’s 1947 version relocates the scene to a car moving through Hollywood, with a crowd on the sidewalks and Einstein astonished by the reception. Carl Seelig’s 1956 biography, citing Plesch, adds still more furniture: a dinner at Chaplin’s villa, a private screening of City Lights, and Einstein’s secretary Helen Dukas and assistant Walther Mayer along for the drive. Each retelling is more circumstantial than the last while resting on the same single second-hand report.

None of which makes the underlying evening fictional. Einstein really was Chaplin’s guest of honour at the City Lights premiere in Los Angeles on 30 January 1931, and the film really did get a standing ovation. It is only the sentence that is unstable.
context.pull: Two men, one ovation, opposite reasons — and by the time it reached the internet it had been credited to the wrong one.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest evidence QI located is Charlie Chaplin's October 1933 article in Woman's Home Companion, in which Chaplin credits the observation about their two kinds of popularity to Einstein's son, not to himself.

The familiar wording 'They're cheering us both, you because nobody understands you, and me because everybody understands me' appears in Janos Plesch's 1947 memoir Janos: The Story of a Doctor, translated by Edward Fitzgerald, Victor Gollancz, London, page 211.
QI states Plesch was not present when the words were spoken, that his account was second-hand, and that the anecdote he told was probably inaccurate.
Einstein had two sons, Hans Albert and Eduard, and QI does not know which one Chaplin meant to credit.
The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (Princeton University Press, ed. Alice Calaprice) includes the line in its 'Others on Einstein' section at page 493, citing Folsing.
City Lights had its gala premiere on 30 January 1931 at the Los Angeles Theater, with Albert Einstein and his wife as guests of honour, and the film received a standing ovation.
The Ultimate Quotable Einstein, edited by Alice Calaprice, is held by the Internet Archive.
Janos Plesch was a Hungarian-born physician and a friend and doctor of Albert Einstein.
Charlie Chaplin lived 16 April 1889 to 25 December 1977 and was a British comic actor and director.
